description: Tech Bird is a software engineering team dedicated to building scalable, data-driven solutions. For the Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots challenge, we developed PyroSync to process and visualize large-scale geospatial satellite data.
summary:
MODIS satellites (Terra and Aqua, 1 km pixels) are nearing the end of their mission, while newer VIIRS sensors (Suomi-NPP, NOAA-20, and NOAA-21, 375 m pixels) detect smaller, cooler fires that MODIS misses. Because raw VIIRS data contains 4.76x to 6.27x more fire pixels than MODIS, combining both records without adjustment makes recent fire seasons look much worse than older ones.

PyroSync fixes this gap in four steps. It standardizes MODIS and VIIRS CSV formats, groups pixels onto an equal-area cosine grid (~1.23 km² and ~123 km² cells), removes weak VIIRS detections under the 6.2 MW MODIS sensitivity limit per overpass, and calculates empirical gain and seasonal Z-score anomalies across years. The web app runs on Go, PostGIS, Next.js, and MapLibre GL JS, serving over 1.04 million NASA FIRMS records from 2010 to 2025 alongside live near real-time updates.
details:
What PyroSync does and how it works

MODIS instruments on Terra and Aqua use 1 km pixels and have provided a global active-fire record for more than two decades, but both satellites are nearing retirement. Newer VIIRS sensors on Suomi-NPP, NOAA-20, and NOAA-21 record at 375 m resolution and pick up smaller, lower-intensity fires. Because of that resolution difference, raw VIIRS pixel counts run 4.76x to 6.27x higher than MODIS. Plotting both feeds together without adjustment creates a sharp artificial spike in fire counts after 2012.

PyroSync aligns both sensor records in four steps, which you can inspect live in the Proof Ladder panel:

  1. Format standardization: Converts MODIS fields (brightness, bright_t31, 0-100 confidence) and VIIRS fields (bright_ti4, bright_ti5, low/nominal/high confidence) into a single UTC schema, deduplicating coordinates to 1e-5 degrees and upgrading Near Real-Time (NRT) records when Standard Processing data arrives.
  2. Equal-area grid aggregation: Assigns detections to cosine-adjusted equal-area cells (~1.23 km² fine cells and ~123 km² regional cells) to prevent high-latitude area distortion. In our 24-hour global seed dataset, this brings the VIIRS to MODIS ratio down from 4.76x to 2.65x.
  3. Overpass grouping and 6.2 MW floor: Groups pixels by cell, satellite, UTC date, and day/night pass, filters out VIIRS cell overpasses below MODIS's 10th-percentile radiative power threshold (6.2 MW), and averages across satellites. That brings the 24-hour seed ratio to 1.12x (and on the full live database of 1,048,084 rows, lowers the global ratio from 6.27x to 1.56x, and Pakistan and the Indus Basin from 3.83x to 1.15x).
  4. Cross-era gain and historical baseline: Calculates an empirical conversion factor (k = 0.66x over 2,600 overlapping days in the Indus Basin) and scores each day against a 2010 to 2025 seasonal baseline (day of year +/- 7 days).

Benefits and impact

Researchers, forestry agencies, and fire analysts can compare older MODIS years with current VIIRS years without false spikes caused by finer sensor resolution. A background poller also checks NASA FIRMS NRT feeds every 60 minutes, and a multi-year calendar highlights abnormal fire seasons by Z-score.

Tools, languages, and setup

The API server and CLI ingestor are written in Go 1.25 (chi, pgx/v5, golang-migrate) backed by PostgreSQL 16 and PostGIS 3.4 for server-side vector tiles (ST_AsMVT). The frontend is built with Next.js 15 (TypeScript static export) and MapLibre GL JS over Esri World Dark Gray Canvas tiles. Everything runs in Docker Compose behind Caddy and Traefik at https://pyrosync.earth.

Edge cases we handled

Incomplete UTC days (is_partial) are marked in the timeline and calendar so a partial current day does not look like a sudden drop in burning activity. On the map, zooming in switches from 123 km² regional grids down to 1.23 km² cells and individual satellite scan-by-track footprints, and Sensor Split mode lets you compare 1 km MODIS footprints directly against 375 m VIIRS pixels.

NASA data

Active-fire records come from NASA FIRMS (MODIS Collection 6.1 and VIIRS 375 m Collection 2 archives and NRT feeds. All matching rules, spatial grid math, bootstrap intervals, and validation checks run directly in Go and PostgreSQL/PostGIS on NASA FIRMS data.
